messages.subject: ERRORS of my stan code
parts:
Hi, I wrote a stan function for poisson multilevel regression with one random intercept and a fixed slope. But I got the error below:
Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
stan::prob::poisson_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Rate parameter[1] is -0.444352:0, but must be >= 0!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.



This is my code:
gene_code<-"
data{   #get the data we have
int <lower=0> N; #number of obs
int <lower=0> J; #number of gene level 
int<lower=0> y[N] ; #y
int<lower=0> x[N];  #x
int <lower=1,upper=J> gene[N];
}
parameters{ #specify the parameter we want to know 
vector[J] a;  #random intercept when gene is the level 
vector[N] epsilon; #amount of dispersion
  
real <lower=0> sigma_a;  #variance of intercept
real <lower=0> sigma_epsilon; #variance of dispersion
real beta;    #common slope;
}
transformed parameters{ #specify the model we will use 
vector[N] y_hat;
for (i in 1:N) 
     y_hat[i] <- a[gene[i]]+beta*x[i]+epsilon[i];#specify the group
}
model { #give the prior distribution 
  beta ~ normal(0,10);
  mu ~ normal(0,1);
  a ~ normal(0, sigma_a);
  epsilon~normal(0,sigma_epsilon);
  y ~ poisson(y_hat); #y and y_hat should have same type 
}
"
N<-dim(table)[1]
J<-dim(table1)[1]
gene<-as.numeric(table$gene)
genelevel<-length(unique(gene))
index<-match(gene, unique(gene)) 
M1_table<-list(N=N, J=J, y=table$envarpfc,
x=table$envarp,gene=index)

fit1<-stan(model_code=gene_code, data=M1_table,
                  iter=1000, chains=4)


Thank you very much!
Shuaqi

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: ERRORS of my stan code
parts:
On Sunday, October 18, 2015 at 9:50:07 PM UTC-4, shuaiqi zhang wrote:
stan::prob::poisson_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Rate parameter[1] is -0.444352:0, but must be >= 0!

I think you want the likelihood to be represented as

y ~ poisson_log(y_hat);

which is to say that the expectation of each element of y is the corresponding element of exp(y_hat).

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: ERRORS of my stan code
parts:
Hi Shuaiqi, it's definitely not the name "y_hat" that's causing any problems. 

I'm not sure, but if you got different results using "y_hat" and "lambda" then it might just be because the initial values were different and the model is sensitive to the initialization. Have you tried simulating fake data and checking if the model (definitely using poisson_log instead of poisson if y_hat is a linear predictor) can recover the parameters?

Jonah

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: ERRORS of my stan code
parts:
Hi Shuaiqi, 

Thanks for sending the code. I haven't been able to replicate the problem you mentioned, so I'm not sure what happened when you were getting those errors. The model as you have it now seems to work ok, but not great. In particular the Rhats and effective sample sizes for lp__ and sigma_epsilon are a bit concerning. 

Instead of epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma_epsilon), I would suggest defining the epsilon vector in transformed parameters as the product sigma_epsilon * epsilon_raw, where epsilon_raw is declared in the parameters block, is the same size as epsilon, and is given standard normal priors (i.e. epsilon_raw ~ normal(0,1)). Statistically this is the same thing as what you currently have but it should help with sampling and I think you'll see the problematic Rhats decrease and effective sample sizes increase.

Jonah

Ther'es not a lot of room for improvement in a simple
regression. It might help to give beta a tighter prior
and sigma_a and sigma_epsilon reasonable priors (at least
weakly informative). But if you have that much data,
it's not likely to matter.

But what you probably want to do is go away from the
characterization of overdispersion with that vector of
epsilons and use a compound distribution like the
negative binomial.

- Bob

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] ERRORS of my stan code
parts:
Hi Shuaiqi, 

That's strange. It doesn't make sense for

rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

to be masked from Rcpp. Those lines are printed as part of RStan's package startup message, advising people that it can be useful to set those options if their system allows it. 

Masking happens because a function/object in one package has the same name as one in a different package that's already loaded, so that when the second package is loaded it "masks" the function in the first package. parts:
This is an issue with how RStan deals with environments.
You must have something non-numerical in your top-level environment
and RStan just converts everything. So it's both inefficient
and unpredictable as written if you don't know what's going to be
in your envioronment. I have no idea if this is fixable on the RStan
side so that it only looks for values in the model, but for now, that's
what happens.

To fix, you need to do one of

a. make sure there's no extraneous non-numerical variables (and ideally no
other variables for efficiency) in the environment from which stan() is called, or

b. explicitly specify the names of variables to read from the environment (all the
data variables), or

c. provide the data as a named list.

- Bob

parts:
I just had a problem with mistakes because I forgot to pass a data variable. There were a bunch of sampling errors, variables being out of range, etc. I was so concerned with my stan code that I didn't think to look in the basic R code.
Is there any warning that a data variable is being taken from the environment, not passed in the data?

Jonah, are you saying that stan() compiles with the data inside, and stan_model() compiles without it?
On Thursday, November 5, 2015 at 4:53:51 PM UTC-5, Jonah wrote:
Bob's right, it's actually going to look in the global environment if you don't specify data.

I had suggested compiling the model first without the data, but I forgot that it looks in the global environment if you don't specify anything. To not use any data, you can use stan_model:

fit0 <- stan_model(file = "model_name.stan")

and then if compilation works you can then sample using the sampling function:

fit <- sampling(fit0, ...)

On Thursday, November 5, 2015 at 4:31:49 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:

This is an issue with how RStan deals with environments.
You must have something non-numerical in your top-level environment
and RStan just converts everything.  So it's both inefficient
and unpredictable as written if you don't know what's going to be
in your envioronment.  I have no idea if this is fixable on the RStan
side so that it only looks for values in the model, but for now, that's
what happens.

To fix, you need to do one of

a.  make sure there's no extraneous non-numerical variables (and ideally no
other variables for efficiency) in the environment from which stan() is called, or

b.  explicitly specify the names of variables to read from the environment (all the
data variables), or

c.  provide the data as a named list.

- Bob

On Wednesday, November 25, 2015 at 3:34:41 PM UTC-5, John Tillinghast wrote:
I just had a problem with mistakes because I forgot to pass a data variable. There were a bunch of sampling errors, variables being out of range, etc. I was so concerned with my stan code that I didn't think to look in the basic R code.
Is there any warning that a data variable is being taken from the environment, not passed in the data?

No, but it should not try to pass any R object that does not have the same name as an object declared in the data block of a Stan file and if you pass in a (partial) list of objects then that will supersede. We need more information about the error you described.

Ben
